title: Spending on experiences versus things
description: Money spent on shared experiences tends to keep paying out in memories long after money spent on objects has faded into the background.

body.heading: Why experiences linger
paragraphs: A new object delights briefly and then becomes part of the furniture of life; we adapt to it quickly. An experience, a trip, a concert, a class taken with a friend, becomes a story, and stories get retold, which means the pleasure repeats for years at no extra cost.
Experiences also connect people. Most treasured memories involve other people, and shared spending buys the setting in which those memories happen.

body.heading: When things are the right buy
paragraphs: The pattern has honest exceptions. A good bicycle is a thing that generates experiences for a decade; a quality tool enables a hundred projects. The useful question is not things or experiences, but whether this purchase will be used, shared and remembered, or merely owned.
Things that remove daily friction, a comfortable chair for someone who reads nightly, a pan that makes cooking pleasant, also keep paying out. Use and memory are the tests, not the category.

body.heading: A gentle spending question
paragraphs: Before a significant purchase, ask: in a year, will I remember this? If the answer is a shrug, the money may work harder saved toward something with a story attached, or spent on time with the people in your stories.
None of this argues for a bare, joyless home. It argues for aiming the fun budget at the purchases that keep being fun after the receipt fades.

takeaway: Ask whether a purchase will be used, shared and remembered; spend where the answer stays yes longest.
